tierWindow.goal: Present with authority and collaborate effectively, and articulate what both are worth to your development as a graduate.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Justification, adaptation and evaluation: assert and defend a position, judge your own and others' contributions, and reflect to improve them.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Ill-defined and contested: a hostile question, a team in conflict, several valid viewpoints at once, with no single settled right answer.
tierWindow.autonomy: Low scaffolding; the learner directs, weighs competing demands, and justifies choices; feedback probes reasoning rather than confirming recall.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner already knows what a presentation is and how one is put together, and can deliver one across common formats. This course assumes that groundwork and moves on to the harder, self-directed concerns: commanding the room, handling challenge, working through group conflict, and articulating the professional value of it all. Teach at the level of a capable finalist preparing for professional practice.

subThemes.label: Presenting with authority: owning your material and projecting confidence rather than reciting prepared lines
Academic voice: asserting and defending your argument, including under difficult questions

Personality types and conflict resolution: using an awareness of difference to find a way through a dispute
Optimising your performance in group work: the practical moves that raise your contribution
Transferable skills and graduate identity: articulating the value of presenting and collaborating through reflection

decidedValue.courseOutcomeCountReason: Three, matching the two threads of the advanced focus plus the articulation that marks this tier out: presenting with authority (the academic-voice thread), collaborating in group work (the teamwork thread), and handling conflict while articulating the professional value of both (the own-development thread that an advanced learner is expected to own). The foundations of what a presentation is and how one is built sit at the introductory tier, and delivering across formats at intermediate, so neither is restated here.

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, presenting with authority: owning your material and defending your argument. Second, collaborating in group work: why the process matters and what tutors look for. Third, conflict and value: using an awareness of personality to resolve disputes, and articulating what the experience is worth. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course is about presenting with authority and collaborating well: the harder half of presenting, once you already know how to build and deliver a talk. By the end you will be able to present with authority and defend your argument, collaborate effectively in group work, and articulate what both are worth to you as a graduate.

These are not polish. The ability to hold a room, answer a hostile question, and work through conflict in a team is exactly what employers test at interview and what professional life demands daily. It is also where the strongest marks, and the real confidence, are found.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: present with authority, collaborate effectively in group work, handle conflict and articulate the value.

practiceConnection.academic: Presenting and group work are where your degree meets professional life most directly. Every pitch, every meeting where views clash, every time you must win a room rather than simply inform it, draws on these skills. Build authority and collaboration now and they carry into interviews, into the teams you will join, and into the judgement your profession will expect of you.

decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Presenting and group work are no longer just tasks to get through. You can present with authority, owning your material and defending your argument when it is challenged. You can collaborate the way tutors and employers value, listening as well as hearing, and taking real responsibility. And you can work through conflict using an awareness of personality, then reflect in a way that judges rather than describes and names what you have gained. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, authority and collaboration are things you practise in every module and every job. Each presentation you own rather than recite, each team you listen within rather than merely join, each conflict you steer rather than avoid, builds the graduate identity employers are looking for. The ability to communicate with authority and work well with others travels into every profession you might enter.

courseReferences.title: See pages 200 to 219 of Chapter 11, 'Creating Effective Presentations and Working in Groups', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
